open_obligations: Check that Kenton et al.'s QuALITY subset is comparable in difficulty to Khan et al.'s HARD subset.
Note different debater models (Gemini Pro 1.5 versus GPT-4-Turbo) and judges.
Check whether Kenton et al. use a quote verification tool.
in.other_title: Extractive tasks: debate gives higher judge accuracy than consultancy and QA without article, except for the weakest judge Gemma7B
in.rationale: Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert LLM judges reach 76% with debate versus 54% with consultancy on QuALITY HARD. Kenton et al. report that on extractive tasks (QuALITY, BoolQ, GPQA-extractive) where only debaters see the article, judges are more accurate under debate than under consultancy and QA without article, except that the weakest judge Gemma7B does no better with debate than with QA without article; both use LLM debaters with privileged article access.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: whether debate beats consultancy for non-expert LLM judges on information-asymmetric reading comprehension

open_obligations: Recompute ASD for Khan et al.'s consultancy runs, if both correct and incorrect assignments were run.
Check that Khan et al.'s debates meet Sudhir et al.'s definition of simultaneous debate.
Check whether the debate-over-consultancy ordering survives under ASD.

Check whether Khan et al.'s judges give probabilities for both answer assignments, since ASD is computed from the judge's belief in a truthful versus a lying agent, while the cited Khan et al. passage reports only accuracies.
in.other_title: Agent score difference (ASD) replaces judge accuracy as the protocol metric
in.rationale: Khan et al. report, for the most persuasive models, non-expert judge accuracy of 88% (humans) and 76% (LLMs) with debate versus 78% and 54% with consultancy. Sudhir et al. argue that judge accuracy relative to consultancy is the wrong alignment metric and that ASD, the score difference between arguing the true and false answer, is equivalent to judge accuracy for simultaneous debate but not for consultancy, so the baseline comparison in previous debate experiments is incorrect; if Khan et al.'s debates are simultaneous, only the consultancy side of the comparison would be affected.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: whether debate's judge-accuracy gain over consultancy measures how much a protocol rewards truth-telling

open_obligations: Check that 'QA without article' matches Khan et al.'s 'Naive' baseline (the authors say it does on p7)
Confirm the Gemma7B exception and the closed-task debate-vs-QA results are not counted as support
in.other_title: Kenton et al. find Khan et al.'s debate-over-consultancy QuALITY result generalises to other tasks
in.rationale: Khan et al. report debate beats consultancy and naive (no-article) judging on QuALITY; the authors explicitly say these results generalise to further extractive tasks and, for debate vs consultancy, to closed tasks. Differences: different models, and debate does not beat QA with article. These are new tasks and models rather than evidence for Khan et al.'s QuALITY figures, so EXTENDS rather than SUPPORTS.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Judge accuracy of debate vs consultancy and vs QA without article, for judges weaker than or equal to the debaters; LLM judges only, so it generalises the direction of Khan et al.'s LLM-judge result (76% with debate for the most persuasive models vs 54% with consultancy) to other tasks and a different set of models, not their human-judge result (88% with debate for the most persuasive models vs 78% with consultancy)

open_obligations: Check whether the capability gap between debaters and judges is information access rather than model capability, and whether Khan et al. list this as a limitation.
Check whether ground truth is used only for evaluation, as sandwiching requires.
Check whether any model is aligned or fine-tuned in an inner loop.
out.other_title: Do debate, market-making and recursive reward modeling work in sandwiching trials?
out.rationale: Bowman et al. ask whether debate can be validated empirically under sandwiching. Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with LLM debate versus 60% naive and 78% consultancy, in an information-asymmetric setup.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate between LLMs helps non-expert judges beyond a baseline, in an information-asymmetric QuALITY HARD setup

open_obligations: Check the different information conditions: whether Khan et al.'s judges see the passage, and how much passage access Parrish et al.'s time-limited judges have.
Check that the naive baseline (60%) is comparable to Parrish et al.'s passage-only condition.
Check the human judge filtering (21 judges after filtering) for selection effects.
out.other_title: Single-turn debate null result is a limited case study, not strong evidence against the usefulness of debate-style set-ups
out.rationale: Parrish et al. say their study is limited in scope and is not strong evidence against the broad potential usefulness of a debate-style set-up. Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate versus 60% naive and 78% consultancy.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether a debate set-up can help non-expert judges on QuALITY when the single-turn human-argument null result is not the whole story

open_obligations: Check whether Parrish et al.'s snippet (PS) baseline is the right analogue of Khan et al.'s naive baseline.
Note the difference between human-written single-turn arguments and LLM debate.
Check judge selection: 21 filtered judges versus MTurk crowdworkers.
out.other_title: Single debate-style arguments were not found to improve human accuracy in the authors' long-context multiple-choice QA set-up
out.rationale: Parrish et al. report human-written single-turn arguments did not improve time-limited judges' accuracy. Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate versus 60% naive on QuALITY HARD. Khan et al.'s setting is information-asymmetric with LLM debaters, while Parrish et al.'s judges have 90 s of passage access and read human-written single-turn arguments (snippets are a separate baseline), so the null and positive results come from different settings.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether debate-style arguments improve accuracy of non-expert judges on hard QuALITY questions

open_obligations: Note that Michael et al.'s AI debate result did not show the gap; check whether debater strength explains the difference.
Check that judge pools and training are comparable.
Check that both use the QuALITY HARD (Gutenberg) questions.
out.other_title: Judge accuracy: human debate 84%, human consultancy 74%, AI debate 78%, AI consultancy 80%
out.rationale: Michael et al. report judge accuracy of 84% for human debate versus 74% for human consultancy, with AI debate at 78% and AI consultancy at 80%. Khan et al. report that, for their most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate versus 78% with consultancy, so a debate-over-consultancy gap appears with model debaters, unlike Michael et al.'s AI debate and consultancy. The two papers ask the same question with different debaters, so Khan et al.'s result is not evidence for the gap Michael et al. found with human debaters.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether debate gives non-expert human judges higher accuracy than consultancy on QuALITY HARD with a hidden passage, with human and AI debaters in Michael et al. and the most persuasive model debaters in Khan et al.

text: For the most persuasive models, the paper reports non-expert human judges achieve 88% and non-expert LLM judges 76% accuracy with debate, where naive performance is 60% and 48% respectively. With the single-model consultancy baseline, human and LLM judges achieve 78% and 54%.
title: Human judges 88% with debate vs 78% consultancy; LLM judges 76% vs 54% (naive 60% / 48%)
